notes:
I could only cover part of Matthew 6. I ran out of search and page-read attempts before I could open Enduring Word, Precept Austin's verse pages, the NET Bible notes or any Catholic site. Pages on John MacArthur's site (gty.org) were blocked. Most notes below therefore come from Wesley (Methodist), the older commentaries on Bible Hub for v. 12, Desiring God, Thomas Watson, MacArthur, the Orthodox Church in America (oca.org), and a few sources on v. 33. I've left out verses where I found nothing.

**v. 1**
- Wesley (Methodist) says chapter 5 described inward holiness, and chapter 6 describes that purity of intention without which none of our outward actions are holy. He takes "righteousness" as a summary word for all good works, and says the warning is against vainglory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- Wesley adds that simply being seen doing good doesn't matter. What Jesus condemns is doing them with this view, to be seen and admired. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- Wesley sees the warning applied to three areas: our neighbour, Matthew 6:2-4 ; to God, Matthew 6:5-6 ; and to ourselves, Matthew 6:16-18. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html

**v. 2**
- Wesley's Sermon 26 says "synagogue" here means any public gathering place, such as the market. He says rich Jews, especially Pharisees, cause a trumpet to be sounded before them in the most public parts of the city before giving. The stated reason was to call the poor together; the real aim was praise. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/
- On "they have their reward," Wesley's Notes say that is All they will have; for they shall have none from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html

**v. 3**
- Wesley reads "left hand… right hand" as a proverb for secrecy. Give as secretly as you can while still giving at all, and still giving in the most effective way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html

**v. 5**
- Wesley says insincerity is the first thing we are to guard against in prayer. He extends this beyond seeking praise: religious acts done for gain are no more acceptable to God than acts done for applause. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/

**v. 6**
- Wesley says "enter into thy closet" means do it with as much secrecy as thou canst. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html

**v. 7**
- Wesley: repeating words you don't mean is vain repetition. We should mean what we say, and the very best prayers are but vain repetitions, if they are not the language of the heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- In his sermon, Wesley warns against thinking a prayer works because it is long, as the pagans did. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/

**v. 8**
- Wesley: we don't pray to tell God what we need. One main purpose of prayer is to prepare us to receive his grace, to exercise our dependence on God; to increase our desire of the things we ask for. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- In the sermon he puts it this way: prayer is less about moving God, who is always more ready to give than you to ask, as to move yourselves. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/

**v. 9**
- Barnes (quoted on StudyLight) calls the prayer a "model." He says it shows the "manner" of praying, evidently not the precise words or petitions which we are to use. He also thinks some petitions may echo Jewish prayers already in use. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/matthew/6-12.html
- Wesley calls it a most perfect and universal form of prayer. He divides it into a preface, petitions and a conclusion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- On "Our Father," Wesley says: if God is a Father, he is good and loving to his children. That is the main reason to pray, because God is willing to bless. "Our" also points to God as Father of all people. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/
- MacArthur (Baptist) sees a structure: the first three petitions are about God, and the last three are about our needs. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/2241

**v. 10**
- Wesley reads "your will be done" as asking that everyone on earth do God's will as willingly as the holy angels, without stopping, and "perfectly as they." This fits his Methodist teaching on holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- He also says God's kingdom is already begun when it is set up in the believer's heart. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/

**v. 11**
- Wesley takes "daily bread" broadly. It means everything soul and body need: not only the meat that perisheth, but the sacramental bread, and thy grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- Ellicott thinks Jesus himself could fitly have prayed this petition, whether we take it in its higher or its lower meaning. https://biblehub.com/matthew/6-12.htm

**v. 12** (traditions differ most here)
- **Common ground:** Gill notes that Jewish writings very often call sins "debts," and that Luke 11:4 says "sins." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/matthew/6-12.html
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** sins are debts we can never repay. He thinks the better Greek text reads "we have forgiven," as a completed act before we begin to pray. In his view, an unforgiving temper proves we haven't grasped how much we owe. https://biblehub.com/matthew/6-12.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** no reason for forgiveness is given in the prayer for the atonement had not yet been made. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/6-12.htm
- **Thomas Watson (Puritan):** forgiving others is not a cause of God's forgiving us, but it is a condition without which he will not forgive us. https://ccel.org/ccel/watson/prayer/prayer.viii.html
- **Desiring God (Reformed Baptist):** sin cannot damn the truly justified. Still, it harms our relationship with God, so believers keep praying this petition. The article also warns that refusing to forgive blocks all our prayers. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/forgive-me-and-help-me-forgive
- **MacArthur (Baptist):** he raises the same question: if all my sins were dealt with at the cross, why do I need to ask forgiveness? I couldn't open the page to read his answer. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/2241
- **Wesley (Methodist):** this verse states the condition and the measure of our forgiveness: All our trespasses and sins are forgiven us, if we forgive, and as we forgive, others. Any bitterness we keep limits how fully God forgives us. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/
- **Orthodox (Fr. Lawrence Farley, OCA):** we need forgiveness daily, which means repenting daily. He says justification is not a single once-for-all event but a continual outpouring for those who keep repenting. He calls the requirement to forgive others absolute, because a closed, hardened heart cannot receive forgiveness. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/the-lords-prayer-forgive-us-our-trespasses
- In short, Reformed writers say past sins can't condemn the justified and frame this petition as about fellowship. Wesley and the Orthodox writer treat forgiving others as a real, ongoing condition of being forgiven.

**v. 13**
- Wesley reads "lead us not into temptation" as: don't let us be overcome, but give us a way to escape and win over sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html
- Wesley explains the closing doxology ("For thine is the kingdom…") as a solemn thanksgiving, a compendious acknowledgement of the attributes and works of God. The BSB text you gave leaves it out. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/

**vv. 14–15**
- Wesley says Jesus stressed this point so strongly that, besides putting it in the prayer, he presently after repeats it twice over. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/sermon-26-upon-our-lords-sermon-on-the-mount-discourse-six/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (on Bible Hub) agree that God will treat our forgiveness exactly as we treat others'. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/6-12.htm
- **Older critical view:** one commentary on Bible Hub (quoting the German scholars Weiss and Meyer) says vv. 14–15 feel out of place after the prayer. It suggests they were probably imported from another connection, e.g., Matthew 18:35. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/6-12.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Wesley notes that Jesus does not enjoin either fasting, alms-deeds, or prayer: all these being duties which were before fully established. On anointing the head, he says to dress as usual. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/matthew-6.html

**vv. 22–23**
- I found only that Wesley preached a separate sermon on these verses, "On a Single Eye" (Sermon 118). I couldn't read it. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-1872-edition/the-sermons-of-john-wesley-biblical-reference/

**v. 33**
- Barnes: seek first to be righteous and to win God's favour, and all necessary things will follow; God will give you what he deems best for you. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/matthew/6-33.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist): if you make God your care, all things necessary for this life shall come to you. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43.xviii.html
- Precept Austin collects devotional quotations on this verse, for example: God who gives you heaven will not deny you your bread on the road thither. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_633-34
- The Bible Says (on Blue Letter Bible) adds a caution against prosperity-style readings: Jesus doesn't promise these things in the time and manner we might prefer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/mat-6-v33.cfm
- All these writers limit "all these things" to necessities. I didn't find any page from a prosperity teacher's own point of view.

**Not found**
- Verses 4 and 18–34 apart from 22–23 and 33.
- Lutheran, Pentecostal and Catholic readings.
- NET Bible or Bible Odyssey scholarship.
- Catholic teaching on "daily bread" as the Eucharist (Wesley's "sacramental bread" note under v. 11 is related).
- Textual notes on the doxology.
- Hyper-grace or prosperity teaching described from those teachers' own pages.

A second round could start with Enduring Word's Matthew 6 page, the Bible Hub commentary pages for each verse, the NET Bible notes on vv. 11 and 13, and newadvent.org on the Lord's Prayer.
